newsitem.title: india: National Conference wins 20 seats in Kashmir poll.
newsitem.headline: National Conference wins 20 seats in Kashmir poll.

text.p: Kashmir's moderate National Conference party swept the first results announced on Tuesday in the troubled Indian state's first local assembly polls in nearly a decade, election officials said.

National Conference leader and former chief minister Farooq Abdullah was elected to the Ganderbal constituency on the edge of Srinagar, the summer capital of India's Jammu and Kashmir state, one of 20 seats the party won in the strife-torn region.
A separatist revolt that began in 1990 has claimed over 20,000 lives, police and hospital sources say.
"It looks like a clean sweep for the National Conference," government spokesman K.B. Jandial told Reuters late on Tuesday.
One seat each was won by Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's Janata Dal party, the Indian National Congress, the Panthers' Party, an independent candidate and a breakaway faction of the Congress party.
The Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) won two seats in the Hindu-dominated Jammu region to the south of the state.
Some of the winning candidates said their first priority would be to work towards restoring peace to the state.
"Restoring normalcy is our top priority," said National Conference's Sadiq Ali, elected from the residential Srinagar area of Zadibal.

"This election is our reply to the Hurriyat leaders," said Mohammed Shafi Bhat, elected from the central Amirakadal precinct. He was referring to the All-Parties' Hurriyat (Freedom) Conference, the umbrella group of separatist parties in the Moslem-dominated Kashmir valley.
The Hurriyat, whose members demand either self-determination or closer ties to Pakistan, had called for a weekend strike in the state to protest the last phase of polls on Monday.
Abdullah, widely tipped to be the state's next chief minister, has repeatedly said he will have no truck with the separatists.
His National Conference is Kashmir's largest political party. The National Conference is leading in more than 20 seats across the state.
The counting of votes began on Tuesday, after the final phase of polling, staggered over a month, ended. Election officials said they expected to have most results by Thursday.
Life in the Kashmir valley returned to normal on Tuesday as judges, teachers, bureaucrats and other government employees returned to work after a 38-day strike to protest the polls.
The strike at state-run institutions was called by the Shoura-e-Jehad, a coalition of five Islamic guerrilla groups.
Many shops and businesses had observed only the brief two-day strike called by the separatist Hurriyat during the final phase of polling at the weekend.
They did brisk trade as Srinagar residents thronged to stock up on essentials soon after they re-opened.
